claims.text: After Executive Validation, the customer usually needs to see or test something before buying. Choose the validation that answers their open question with the least time and risk.
claims.checked_by: Studio author: drafted from the cited source text; no verbatim excerpt recorded; SME verification pending

claims.text: Ask what is still uncertain for the buyer. Then pick the option that resolves it, considering: The question: "Will this workflow make sense to my team?" or "Will it work with our specific systems and permissions?" The data needed: sample, representative, or the customer's own. The audience: an executive, a few power users, or a broader cohort. Preparation and effort, for the customer and for Glean. Risk: data handling, security review, and expectations.

claims.text: Glean's technical validation guidance sets out three option types, increasing in preparation and duration: custom tailored demos, a sandbox, and a pilot or proof of concept. Glean's refreshed Blueprint material also positions a Glean Lab as the default validation event after Executive Validation. If the buyer needs to understand the future workflow, a tailored demo or a Lab scenario may be enough. If they need proof of behavior on specific enterprise integrations or data, define exactly what evidence a more involved evaluation must produce.
claims.checked_by: Fact Integrity Auditor (studio spot check)

claims.text: Glean sources emphasize different defaults. Refreshed material favors the Glean Lab, while some sales enablement favors tailored demos. Teach the principle: use the lightest option that credibly resolves the remaining buying uncertainty. No single option is right regardless of the question.

claims.text: Glean's validation-events training explains why pilots usually convert: by the time a pilot can start, the security review, the Blueprint, the economic buyer's priorities, executive buy-in, pricing and budget conversations, and IT readiness have typically already happened. The conversion comes from that groundwork, not from the pilot itself. A heavier option chosen to compensate for missing groundwork adds cost without adding certainty. Custom tailored demo Shows the future workflow; least effort Sandbox Hands-on use with selected content Pilot or proof of concept Real systems for a defined co

claims.text: After Executive Validation, the only open question is whether the support team will understand and accept the proposed workflow. Recommend a validation path.

claims.text: A tailored demo or a suitable Glean Lab scenario, built around the prioritized support workflow, with clear success questions. For example: "Can agents find the approved answer for these five representative case types, and would they use this flow?" Escalate to a heavier option only if this can't answer the buying question, and document why the extra investment is needed.

claims.text: The validation options differ in what data they use, how faithfully they reflect permissions, who can use them, and what their results can prove. Know the differences, and check the current details before you offer one.

claims.text: Tailored demo | Prepared scenario, often sample data | How the future workflow could look | Behavior on the customer's own systems and permissions Glean Lab | Curated or sample-data experience | Hands-on feel for the prioritized tasks | Production fidelity Sandbox | Sample data, plus customer-uploaded test content where permitted | Hands-on use with selected content | Personalization or permissions at production fidelity Pilot or proof of concept | The customer's systems and data, scoped | Behavior with real integrations, for a defined cohort | A full rollout's adoption or value

claims.text: Before offering an option, write down its current, approved description: data type, permission fidelity, allowed users, duration, setup owner, security, cost, and what the result can prove. Environment details change between versions of Glean's guides. For example, sandbox access, data options, and limits have been described differently over time. Flag any differences you find. Boundary Don't teach dated pricing, revenue thresholds, shared-login behavior, or environment limits as permanent facts. Confirm the live terms with the Glean account team before offering an option to a customer.

claims.text: Teams use these names inconsistently, so confirm what each person means. The same training notes that a customer can separately purchase a sandbox instance after becoming a customer, which is different from a sandbox used for validation. The training also clarifies the data behind the lighter options. A custom demo late in the sale often uses customer files that have been uploaded, and the sandbox uses uplo

claims.text: Glean's sandbox guidance starts with alignment. Validate the pain, the rough order of magnitude, and the sandbox's purpose as technical validation with the economic buyer. Set the expectation that the sandbox won't show personalization or the knowledge graph.

claims.text: Start with the pain and the value, highlight the differentiators that matter, give a custom demo, then hand over to hands-on use. Boundary Follow the current approved access and data-handling rules. Never upload sensitive information. claims.text: Glean's guidance expects the following before a pilot: The three whys are answered: why change, why now, why Glean. Technical use cases and a test plan are documented and mutually agreed. Measurable success criteria are agreed with the customer, and the scope, timeline, impact, and test plan are defined.

claims.text: The same guide sets out non-negotiable rules: No approval, no pilot. Leadership approval is required. No signed pilot order form, no pilot. claims.text: Agree in advance what happens if things change. If a test fails because the intended source is unavailable, that calls for a decision about the dependency.
